title: Diwali Arrives With Worsening Air: How To Celebrate More Safely
excerpt: Firecracker smoke adds fine particles to already polluted winter air. Here is who faces the highest risk, how to read the AQI, and the mask, indoor-air and activity steps clinicians recommend.
body:
• Diwali coincides with the onset of winter air pollution in northern India, and firecrackers add fine particles to air already burdened by traffic, industry, construction dust and farm-waste burning.
  • On India's AQI scale, 201-300 is 'poor', 301-400 is 'very poor' and above 500 is 'severe'; check your local AQI before planning time outdoors.
  • Children, older adults and people with asthma, COPD, heart disease or diabetes face the highest risk; a well-fitting N95 filters at least 95% of airborne particles, an N99 at least 99%.
  • The safer-celebration steps are concrete: limit outdoor time in smoke, keep windows closed, run a HEPA purifier in the room you use most, and skip outdoor exercise when pollution peaks.

Diwali begins this Sunday, and across northern India it arrives with the season's worst air. The festival's fireworks land on top of pollution already driven by industrial emissions, heavy traffic, construction dust and the burning of agricultural waste, held close to the ground by stagnant winter air and weak winds, Policy-Wire reported.

"Poor air quality is a perennial issue in the region," Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, told Policy-Wire, adding that firecrackers further worsen the ongoing crisis. In Delhi, fine particle levels last year averaged 19 times the limit set by the World Health Organization, with monitors frequently hitting maximum readings, the report said.

Who is most at risk

Children and older adults are the groups clinicians name first. Children's developing lungs and faster breathing rates mean they can inhale more pollutants relative to their body weight, and exposure can trigger coughing, wheezing and asthma flare-ups, Max Healthcare advises. For older adults, the risk compounds when reduced lung function coincides with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), heart disease or diabetes; fine particulate matter can enter the lungs and add stress to the cardiovascular system.

Firecrackers release PM2.5 and PM10 along with gases; PM2.5 particles are small enough to reach deep into the lungs. Prolonged exposure is linked to persistent coughing, airway inflammation and asthma attacks, Policy-Wire reported. Even so-called green crackers are not harmless: lower emissions can still provoke symptoms in vulnerable people.

Read the AQI before you plan

India's AQI system bands the risk plainly: readings between 201 and 300 are classified as "poor," 301 to 400 are "very poor," and levels above 500 are considered "severe," posing a threat even to otherwise healthy individuals, according to Policy-Wire. Check government or private monitoring data before outdoor gatherings, walks or games, and postpone prolonged outdoor activity when levels are high — particularly for children with asthma and older adults with heart or lung conditions.

The safer-celebration playbook

Mask properly outdoors. Dr. Arvind Kumar, a chest surgeon at Medanta and founder of the Lung Care Foundation, advises N95 or N99 respirators during high pollution: an N95 is engineered to block at least 95% of airborne particles and an N99 at least 99%, though neither filters harmful gases. The mask must cover the nose, mouth and chin with the nose clip sealed tight; facial hair can break the seal, and loose surgical masks or cloth scarves provide unreliable protection against fine particles. The US Environmental Protection Agency's smoke guidance makes the same fit point: choose a NIOSH-approved particulate respirator marked "N95" or "P100" with two straps around the head, and note that respirators do not come in sizes suitable for very young children. Children under two and people with heart or lung conditions should seek medical advice on mask use, Policy-Wire reported.

Protect indoor air. Close windows and doors during heavy smoke, and run a portable air purifier with a HEPA filter in the room where the family spends the most time, sized for that room. Avoid adding indoor smoke: incense, mosquito coils and candles release particles that linger for hours, Max Healthcare and Policy-Wire both advise. Mopping floors instead of sweeping avoids stirring settled particles back into the air.

Change the activity, not the festival. Avoid strenuous exercise outdoors, especially in the early morning when pollution often peaks. Keep time near firecracker displays short, watch fireworks from away from the immediate smoke where possible, and keep prescribed inhalers and medicines accessible for family members with asthma or COPD, following their existing treatment plan.

Individual precautions have limits, Narayan noted — masks and filters reduce exposure but cannot substitute for cleaner air. Seek medical attention promptly for persistent coughing, breathlessness, chest tightness or pain, or asthma symptoms that do not ease with a prescribed reliever, Max Healthcare advises.
